extracted.intended_audience: readers and fans of noir/crime fiction; general readers seeking a list of top noir authors (and aspiring noir writers looking for exemplars)
extracted.subtask_description: A listicle-style overview naming twenty prominent noir fiction writers and describing the characteristic features of their work; intended as a survey of practitioners and exemplars of the noir/hardboiled tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dark and gritty realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir fiction is characterized by its use of dark and gritty realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly emphasizes 'dark and gritty realism' as a core genre trait and cites authors (e.g., Raymond Chandler, Dashiell Hammett, Jim Thompson, David Goodis) whose work embodies this realism in prose, setting, and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of moral ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir fiction explores moral ambiguity; characters and situations resist clear moral judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple entries note 'moral ambiguity' and 'morally compromised' characters (top paragraph, Chandler, Cain, Highsmith, Block). Used as a key evaluative quality when judging noir works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unconventional narrative structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir often uses unconventional narrative structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction mentions 'often a use of unconventional narrative structures'; specific authors (e.g., David Goodis) are noted for experimentation with form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban setting / atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir is usually set in urban environments and features urban decay and the city's underbelly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genre is described as 'usually set in urban environments' (Chandler's Los Angeles, Raymond Chandler; Raymond-centric 'urban underbelly'; Derek Raymond's London; Ellroy's Los Angeles). Atmospheric evocation of city/setting is treated as central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flawed and morally compromised characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are flawed and morally compromised; protagonists frequently struggle with inner demons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly notes flawed protagonists (e.g., 'flawed and morally compromised', 'amoral Frank Chambers', 'charming but sociopathic conman Tom Ripley'). Depth of character moral conflict is an evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Economical, sharp, and often hardboiled dialogue is a key stylistic feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several author descriptions highlight 'sharp dialogue' or 'tough-talking' lines (Chandler, Cain, Hammett, Block). Dialogue quality is presented as a marker of strong noir prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cynical worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: A cynical, disillusioned worldview appears across classic noir works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening and author descriptions (Chandler, Hammett, Spillane) stress cynicism and disillusionment as tonal hallmarks that inform voice and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gritty, pared-down prose style
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose that is direct, simple, and gritty — often understated rather than ornate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammett's 'simple and direct' prose and 'gritty prose' (Chandler) are cited as stylistic models; this is presented as an evaluative quality for noir writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir often delivers psychological complexity and interiority in characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes 'psychological depth' (intro, Highsmith) and authors like Jim Thompson and Patricia Highsmith are given as exemplars of psychologically complex, suspenseful character studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intricate / clever plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-woven, intricate plots and tight plotting are valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chandler's 'ability to weave intricate plots' and Block's 'clever plots' are cited; plot complexity and craft are repeatedly mentioned as strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of social and racial issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir can and does interrogate social and racial dynamics within its settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors such as Chester Himes (Harlem crime novels) and Walter Mosley (race relations and social commentary) are cited; inclusion of social critique is an evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vernacular and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic use of regional or racial vernacular/voice to render character and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Himes's 'use of black vernacular' is highlighted as a stylistic and cultural strength; voice authenticity is therefore a criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unflinching portrayal of violence and betrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct, often brutal depiction of violence, betrayal, and dark deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cain and Thompson are noted for 'unflinching portrayal of violence and betrayal' and dark, destructive character arcs; realism in depictions of crime is part of the genre's evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bleak / nihilistic worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: A bleak, sometimes nihilistic outlook pervades certain noir works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derek Raymond's 'nihilistic worldview' and general descriptions of bleakness signal that tonal bleakness is characteristic and can be a measure of noir intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark humour / wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of dark humor or wry wit within a grim setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Willeford's 'dark and humorous' novels and mentions of 'dark humour' (Megan Abbott) show that ironic or black comedy is an acknowledged element of some noir writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric, place-driven settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong sense of place and atmosphere that shapes mood and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ann Cleeves's 'atmospheric settings' and many authors' reliance on setting (LA, Harlem, Melbourne, Shetland Islands) indicate that atmosphere is a key evaluative feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong social and political commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir can function as social or political critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walter Mosley's work is singled out for 'strong social and political commentary'; the genre's engagement with justice, race, and class is a criterion for assessing depth and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspenseful and psychologically complex plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plotting that builds suspense and foregrounds psychological complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highsmith's 'suspenseful and psychologically complex novels' are invoked; suspense mechanics plus psychological nuance are combined evaluative aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-bending and imaginative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who blend noir with other genres or use imaginative, nontraditional approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michael Chabon is described as 'imaginative and often genre-bending'; willingness to hybridize or innovate is presented as a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive perspective (e.g., female viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing a distinctive or underrepresented viewpoint to crime/noir fiction (for example, female perspectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Megan Abbott's work is noted for drawing 'from classic subgenres ... from a female perspective'; perspective diversity is an evaluative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and regional specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic portrayal of local/regional milieus and social textures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ted Lewis's Melbourne settings and their authenticity are cited; fidelity to regional detail strengthens noir resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolific versatility / range
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth of output and ability to write across subgenres (versatility and productivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawrence Block's 'versatility' and publication of over 80 books is presented as evidence of craft and range; prolific, versatile authors are flagged as important practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic hardboiled tropes (private eye, tough-guy PI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of hardboiled detective protagonists and related genre tropes (private investigators, femme fatales, corrupt power brokers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chandler's Philip Marlowe, Hammett's Sam Spade, and Spillane's Mike Hammer are cited as archetypes; presence or inventive use of these tropes is a metric for genre fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of corruption and institutional decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives that expose corruption, institutional rot, and systemic wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Ellroy's focus on 'corruption and the dark side of human nature' and other authors' attention to power structures mark this as an important dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural impact / adaptability to other media
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that have had significant cultural impact or successful adaptations (films, TV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cain's and Goodis's novels being adapted into iconic films ('Double Indemnity', 'Shoot the Piano Player') are cited as signs of lasting influence; impact/adaptability is presented as a measure of significance.
